items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn (~25 in 1870) makes his first adult appearance in this enumeration. Also search for Thomas Flynn (~55–65 if born c. 1805–1815), who headed the household in 1850 (a_005) and 1860 (a_010). If Thomas still heads a household and Patrick remains in it, this extends the co-residence pattern from two censuses to three — strengthening the father-son identification. If Patrick has formed his own household, his enumeration district and neighbors may still place him geographically near Thomas. FamilySearch collection 1438024 (United States Census, 1870; 38.5 million persons; name-searchable). Search both Flynn and spelling variants (Flinn, Flin).

Ancestry maintains an independent index of the 1870 federal census for Schuylkill County (ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/). Search here if FamilySearch returns no match or ambiguous results — different transcribers may render the Flynn surname as Flinn, Flin, or Flyon, surfacing entries the FamilySearch index missed.

The 1880 census is the most probative in this plan: it is the first federal enumeration to record each person's explicit relationship to the head of household. If Thomas Flynn (now ~65–75) still heads a household and Patrick (~35) appears in it with the relationship 'Son,' the relationship column is direct, stated evidence of parentage — converting the inferred co-residence of 1850 (a_004) and 1860 (a_010) into an explicit parent-child assertion. Even if Patrick heads his own household by 1880, a separate search for Thomas in the same county may locate Thomas's entry and confirm he survived into this enumeration. FamilySearch collection 1417683 (United States Census, 1880; 50.1 million persons; name-searchable). Search both Flynn and spelling variants.

Ancestry's independent 1880 index (ancestry.com/search/collections/6742/) as a fallback if FamilySearch yields no match for Patrick or Thomas Flynn. MyHeritage (collection 10132) provides a tertiary option if both FamilySearch and Ancestry fail. The 1880 relationship column is too important to leave unsearched because of a single index's transcription gap.

The 1890 census was largely destroyed by fire and is unavailable — 1900 is the next surviving enumeration. Patrick (~55) is known to have died 12 March 1908 (a_011), so he should appear in the 1900 count. The 1900 schedule is especially valuable for this question: it records father's birthplace and mother's birthplace in dedicated columns. If Patrick's entry names Ireland (or a specific Irish county) as his father's birthplace, it corroborates the Irish origin implied by the 1850 and 1860 censuses and consistent with Thomas Flynn heading an Irish immigrant household. The schedule also records month and year of birth and immigration year, which may help resolve the conflict between the census-reported Ireland birthplace (a_002, a_009) and the death certificate's Pennsylvania (a_012, secondary informant). FamilySearch collection 1325221 (United States Census, 1900; 76.2 million persons; name-searchable).

Ancestry's independent 1900 index for Schuylkill County (ancestry.com/search/collections/7884/). Search here if FamilySearch yields no match — name variants (Flinn, Flin) may be captured differently. The parental-birthplace columns make this census year too valuable to forgo because of a single index gap.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.
Roman Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Scranton was erected in 1868; sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: First plan for q_001. Starting point: the 1850 US Census (src_001) places Patrick Flynn (~5, b. Ireland) in Thomas Flynn's household, but the 1850 census does not state relationships — the father-son link is inferred from household position and shared surname, not reported by any informant. No mother has been identified in any extracted assertion. This plan targets the records most likely to confirm or deny Thomas Flynn's parentage of Patrick and to identify the mother. BCG Standard 11 flag: the assumption that Thomas is Patrick's father is not yet documented — plan items 1-2 are designed to test it directly.

Patrick Flynn died in 1908. Pennsylvania civil registration began in 1906 (loc_001), so a state death certificate should exist for his 1908 death. Pennsylvania death certificates routinely request the deceased's parents' names and birthplaces; the informant's proximity to those facts determines reliability (a child informant is likely to know; a neighbor may report 'unknown'). This is the highest-priority direct evidence of parentage available in the Pennsylvania record base. Search Ancestry's Pennsylvania death records index for Patrick Flynn / Flyn / Flinn, death year 1908, Schuylkill County.

The 1880 US Census was the first to record each person's relationship to the head of household explicitly ('son,' 'daughter,' etc.). In 1880 Patrick would be approximately 35; he may still be in Thomas's household or have established his own. If still in Thomas's household, the 1880 entry would directly state 'son' — corroborating the parent-child link that the 1850 census only implies. Even if Patrick has his own household by 1880, searching Thomas Flynn's household that year identifies surviving family members and narrows the mother's identity. The 1880 census is fully indexed on FamilySearch. Search Thomas Flynn / Flinn / Flyn and Patrick Flynn / Flinn / Flyn, Schuylkill County.

In 1860 Patrick would be approximately 15 and almost certainly still in Thomas Flynn's household. While the 1860 census does not state relationships, continued co-residence over a decade corroborates the inferred parent-child relationship from 1850. This record is also likely to reveal the mother's name and any siblings not apparent from the 1850 extraction. The 1860 census is fully indexed on FamilySearch. Search for Thomas Flynn / Flinn / Flyn, Schuylkill County.

In 1870 Patrick would be approximately 25 — he may still reside with Thomas or have established his own household. Searching both Thomas Flynn's household and Patrick Flynn's own household that year tracks the family's continued presence in Schuylkill County, may identify the mother if still living, and covers the gap between the 1860 and 1880 censuses. The 1870 census is fully indexed on FamilySearch. Search for Thomas Flynn and Patrick Flynn / Flinn / Flyn, Schuylkill County.

Dedicated search for the parents' marriage — required for every parentage plan. The Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 982,415 indexed persons, 1708-1985) is the primary source for Catholic parish marriage entries; the Flynn family was likely Irish Catholic (Diocese of Philadelphia to 1868, Diocese of Scranton thereafter — loc_001). Their marriage entry: (a) confirms Thomas and his wife as a couple; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name, which census records and death certificates typically omit; and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth, corroborates the family unit. Limit: the marriage proves the couple married and dates their union — it is not, by itself, evidence that Patrick is their child; a record placing Patrick with both parents is still needed. Date window covers a plausible marriage before Patrick's ~1845 birth through the period end. If the couple married in Ireland before emigrating, this item may yield nothing; that would trigger an Ireland locality survey. Search for Thomas Flynn / Flinn / Flyn in SYNTH-PA-CHURCH.

Browse fallback for item 5 (pli_005): image group 007936751 (Schuylkill County Church Records, 1842-1895, 0% indexed, bilingual English/German). If the indexed SYNTH-PA-CHURCH search yields no marriage entry for Thomas Flynn, browse this volume for Flynn / Flinn / Flyn marriage entries. The German-language content reflects the county's Lutheran and Reformed populations; the Flynn family is expected in the English-language Catholic registers. Browse image by image.

Search the indexed Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 982,415 persons, 1708-1985) for baptisms of Patrick Flynn's siblings born to Thomas and his wife in Pennsylvania after the family's arrival (~1848-1850). A baptism entry directly names both parents — the strongest church-record evidence of parentage. Patrick's own ~1845 baptism almost certainly occurred in Ireland before emigration and is outside this collection's reach, but younger siblings born in Schuylkill County would be found here and would name Thomas and his wife as parents. Search Flynn / Flinn / Flyn, birth years 1848-1875.

Browse fallback for item 7 (pli_007): image group 007936751 (Schuylkill County Church Records, 1842-1895, 0% indexed, bilingual English/German). If the indexed SYNTH-PA-CHURCH search yields no baptism entries for Flynn children, browse this same volume for entries naming Thomas or Patrick Flynn as father or child. The English-language Catholic registers are the target; German-language entries may incidentally contain Irish names if a parish served a mixed congregation.

If Thomas Flynn died in Schuylkill County, his will or estate administration record would name his heirs — direct evidence of parentage. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (1999196) returned personCount 0, confirming it is a browse-only image collection with no name-searchable index. Volume 007936749 covers Schuylkill County Probate Records 1851-1930 (0% indexed). Date range is bounded by Thomas's estimated lifespan as the record's creator (born ~1810-1820, plausibly dying 1851-1905), not by Patrick's research window. Browse image by image in the Register of Wills dockets for Thomas Flynn / Flinn / Flyn.

Thomas Flynn was an Irish immigrant who would have naturalized in Pennsylvania. Volume 007936750 covers Schuylkill County Naturalization Records 1849-1915 (0% indexed — browse only). Post-1906 naturalization petitions explicitly name the petitioner's wife and children by name; earlier declarations of intent may name the applicant's Irish county or townland of origin. As a Schuylkill County resident by 1850, Thomas likely filed his declaration of intent in the early-to-mid 1850s and completed naturalization by the 1860s-1870s. Date window bounded by Thomas's likely active naturalization period. Browse for Thomas Flynn / Flinn / Flyn.

Required FAN-cluster item for a parentage question (BCG Standard 14). Volume 007936752 covers Schuylkill County Deed Records 1815-1900 (22% indexed). If Thomas Flynn purchased or sold land, deed records name the grantor and grantee plus witnesses — frequently kin — and the boundary recital names adjacent landowners, a source of FAN names not available from census or church records alone. Purchasers at estate sales also appear in related probate deeds and may corroborate family relationships. Date window set to Thomas's lifespan as the likely property owner (born ~1810-1820 to ~1905). Because only 22% of the volume is indexed, if a name search yields nothing, browse deed books covering Thomas's active years (circa 1850-1885). Search for Thomas Flynn / Flinn / Flyn.

entry.rationale: An uncited FamilySearch tree source (no attached record) places an 'M M Wood' household in the 1860 Blount County, Alabama census — matching Martha's birth year (~1859) and stated birth state (Georgia). BCG Standard 11 requires verifying this starting-point fact before building on it. If confirmed, the household head is Martha's probable father and the listed wife her probable mother; both names, ages, birthplaces, and co-resident siblings appear on the same census page — the single record most likely to name both parents at once. Search on surname 'Wood' in Blount County, Alabama in 1860 using FamilySearch collection 1927240 (United States Census Population Schedules, 1860; personCount 23M, name-searchable); volume 005154190 covers Blount County and is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable. Try spelling variants (Woode, Woods) if Wood alone yields nothing.

The 1879 Hill County marriage shows Martha styled as a widow — the widow styling refers to the Lanham marriage (W F Lanham), not necessarily to 'Wood' being a prior married name. Even so, whether the 1869 Lanham marriage was Martha's FIRST has not been established. If she had an even earlier marriage in Smith County before 1869, 'Wood' on the Lanham record would be a prior married name rather than her birth surname, fundamentally changing which Wood family to search in Alabama. Per loc_002, Smith County marriage volumes 1857-1876 (FamilySearch vol. 007255720) and 1875-1889 (vol. 007255721) are 100% name-indexed and full-text searchable. Search for any bride with given name beginning 'M' in Smith County before 7 Jan 1869. A nil result here meaningfully raises confidence that 'Wood' is Martha's birth surname and the 1869 Lanham marriage was her first.

Martha married W F Lanham in Smith County on 7 Jan 1869. By the June 1870 census she would appear as Mrs. M J Lanham in the Lanham household. The 1870 census records each person's birthplace — a 'Georgia' entry for Martha directly corroborates her identity as the Georgia-born child later found in the Alabama Wood household (Item 1), and her stated age (~21 in 1870) calibrates the ~1859 birth estimate. W F Lanham's property and occupation entries may surface additional county records worth searching. Search on surname 'Lanham' (and variants: Landham, Lannam) in Smith County, Texas in the FamilySearch 1870 census collection.

Martha married James M Neal on 31 Jul 1879 in Hill County, Texas and would appear in his household in the June 1880 census. The 1880 census uniquely records each person's father's birthplace AND mother's birthplace — Martha's two parent-birthplace fields narrow the geographic origin of the Wood parents even before they are identified directly. Her own stated birthplace (Georgia) and age (~21) provide a further calibration check. Search on surname 'Neal' with given name 'Martha' or 'Mattie' in Hill County, Texas. If not found in Hill County, broaden to adjacent Texas counties.

If Item 1 confirms the M M Wood household in Blount County, the 1870 census shows whether the parents and remaining siblings stayed in Alabama after Martha departed for Texas (she married in Smith County, Texas in Jan 1869). A father born ~1820-1835 would be 35-50 in 1870 and highly likely still living; a surviving 1870 entry for the Wood household confirms the parents' names, ages, and birthplaces and identifies any siblings still at home — corroborating the family unit identified in 1860. Search surname 'Wood' in Blount County, Alabama in the FamilySearch 1870 census; if not found there, broaden to statewide Alabama.

A parentage question requires a dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other. If Item 1 identifies the Wood household head, his marriage record names the mother's maiden name (assuming this was his first and only marriage — a caveat to note if multiple Wood marriages appear). Additionally, siblings' marriage records in Blount County often name the father and sometimes the mother, providing corroborating parentage statements. Date range sized to the father's plausible marriage years: a father born ~1820-1835 would likely have married ~1835-1850. Search surname 'Wood' in FamilySearch collection 1598408 (Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950; personCount 1.2M, name-searchable) and Blount County marriage volume 007316662 (92% name-indexed, full-text searchable per loc_001).

No civil death records exist for Blount County before 1908 (loc_001). If Martha's father died in Alabama, a probate or estate administration file is the primary alternative: a will naming 'Martha' or 'M J' as a daughter, or an administration listing her as an heir, is direct parentage evidence. A father born ~1820-1835 could plausibly have died anywhere from 1860 to ~1905 — the date range is sized to the father's lifespan, not Martha's own research window. Per loc_001, Blount County probate records (1845-1957) are available on FamilySearch collection 1537764 (Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985; personCount 438K, name-searchable) and volume 004808801; the volume is only 2% name-indexed but IS full-text searchable, so keyword search for 'Wood' (and 'Martha', 'M J') is required rather than a standard name search.

FAN item — W F Lanham (Martha's first husband) died between 7 Jan 1869 (marriage date) and 31 Jul 1879 (date Martha remarried as 'widow'). His estate file or administration record names Martha as widow, corroborating her identity as M J Lanham and pinning her location in the intervening decade. A probate file might also state Martha's full given name or a residence that narrows where her Wood family lived. Date range sized to the creator's (Lanham's) plausible death window. Search FamilySearch collection 2272001 (Texas, Probate Case Files, 1800-1990; personCount 612K, name-searchable) on 'Lanham' and variants in Smith County, Texas. Per loc_002, no civil death registration existed in Texas before 1903, so probate is the principal documentary trace of Lanham's death.

Martha was born ~1859 in Georgia; her family had moved to Alabama by the 1860 census. In 1850, the Wood parents were in Georgia — a 1850 Georgia census entry would show the family a decade before the Alabama move, naming parents with ages and birthplaces, and listing older siblings born before 1850 whose ages and birthplaces corroborate the family unit. Ancestry.com holds the 1850 U.S. Census with strong Georgia indexing (external link returned by external_links_search for Blount County). Search on surname 'Wood' in Georgia in the 1850 census, filtering to households with a head of approximate age to be the father of a child born ~1859. Ancestry's Blount County Alabama records (https://www.ancestry.com/search/locations/blount-county-alabama) should also be checked for supplemental cemetery and church records not held on FamilySearch, including FindAGrave memorials for Wood family members in Blount County cemeteries.

dimensions.rationale: The plan is factually sound in most respects — jurisdictions, collections, and record types are accurate for the time period. However, there is one critical tool-call error: the place_search call for 'United States' returned fixture_not_found, indicating incorrect tool usage. This error did not prevent the plan from being written (the skill recovered by using place names already in the project context), but it represents a failure in tool argument construction. The persisted plan itself is substantively correct — all 9 items target appropriate records, jurisdictions exist in the target period, and the rationales accurately describe what each record type would reveal. dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The skill addressed everything the user message and input state required. It created the first research plan for q_002 (Add-new path, since no prior plan existed), included 9 plan items covering the full scope of the parentage question, and persisted the plan to research.json with all required fields. dimensions.name: Record type selection
dimensions.rationale: Every plan item targets appropriate record types for the parentage question. Census records (pli_001, pli_003, pli_004, pli_005, pli_009) answer identity and geographic questions. Vital records (pli_002, pli_006) directly name parents or test whether 'Wood' is Martha's birth surname. Probate records (pli_007, pli_008) provide parentage evidence when civil death records don't exist. Each rationale explains what specific information the record type provides: pli_001 notes the census 'single record most likely to name both parents at once'; pli_002 explains that an earlier marriage would change which Wood family to search; pli_006 states the marriage record 'names the mother's maiden name'; pli_007 notes a will or administration 'is direct parentage evidence.' The selection is defensible and well-justified.

dimensions.name: Objective scope containment
dimensions.rationale: Every item's rationale ties it to evidence about Martha J, the question's subject. Items targeting relatives' records (pli_008 on W F Lanham's estate) explicitly state what they would reveal about Martha: 'names Martha as widow, corroborating her identity as M J Lanham and pinning her location in the intervening decade.' Census items (pli_003, pli_004) focus on Martha's own entries and what they reveal about her parents' birthplaces. The plan does not pursue a relative's own missing facts — it pursues records that name or identify Martha's parents. No item's deliverable is a relative's own record for its own sake. The scope is tightly contained to the parentage question.

dimensions.name: Sequencing logic
dimensions.rationale: The sequence reflects defensible research logic. Free/indexed sources come early: pli_001 (1860 census, 99% indexed, free), pli_002 (Smith County marriages, 100% indexed, free), pli_003–pli_005 (census records, free). Narrow before broad: Smith County (where Martha married) before statewide Alabama searches. The plan identifies a critical dependency: pli_002 (earlier marriage search) must run early because 'if she had an even earlier marriage in Smith County before 1869, Wood on the Lanham record would be a prior married name rather than her birth surname, fundamentally changing which Wood family to search in Alabama.' This dependency is explicit in the rationale. The date ranges reach the later part of Martha's window: pli_007 extends to 1905 (covering the father's plausible lifespan, not just Martha's birth window). No item waits on evidence only a later item can produce. The 1850 Georgia census (pli_009) comes last, as a supplemental search after the primary Alabama leads. Fallback chains are implicit in the structure (if pli_001 fails, pli_005 and pli_006 provide alternative paths to the Wood family). The sequencing is sound.

dimensions.name: Jurisdiction accuracy
dimensions.rationale: All jurisdictions are correct for the target periods. Blount County, Alabama (formed 1818, stable through 1860–1880) is correctly identified. Smith County, Texas (formed 1846) and Hill County, Texas (formed 1853) both existed in their target periods (1869, 1879). Georgia existed in 1850. The plan correctly notes that 'No boundary change splits Blount County (formed 1818, stable)' and that 'Texas did not require statewide civil registration of births/deaths until 1903; pre-1903 events rely on church, cemetery, marriage, and probate records.' The plan also correctly identifies that 'No civil death records exist for Blount County before 1908 (loc_001),' which is why probate is prioritized. All jurisdictions match what existed in the time periods being searched.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.
Roman Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Scranton was erected in 1868; sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: The 1880 U.S. census is the first federal enumeration to include a relationship column, making it the highest-priority source to search. If Patrick Flynn (born ~1845, age ~35 in 1880) remains in or near Thomas Flynn's household, his relationship would be stated as 'son' for the first time — providing the direct parentage evidence currently lacking from the 1850 and 1860 census co-residences (which infer the relationship only). Even if Patrick has left the household, Thomas's wife (Patrick's mother) would appear with her name recorded for the first time in any source; her name is entirely unknown from all prior searches. Thomas (born ~1818) would be ~62. The proof summary (ps_001) explicitly names this census as a primary remaining gap. Try name variants: Flinn, Flynd, Flynn.

The 1870 U.S. census fills the gap between the confirmed 1860 Flynn household (pli_004, completed) and the 1880 census. Thomas (born ~1818) would be ~52; Patrick (born ~1845) would be ~25 and may have begun his own household. The 1870 census does not state relationships, but Thomas's wife would appear by name if she was alive — providing the first opportunity to identify Patrick's mother from US records. It also shows whether Patrick remained in the Flynn household into young adulthood, which corroborates the parent-child relationship. The proof summary (ps_001) identifies this census as a primary gap. Try name variants: Flinn, Flynd.

The 1900 U.S. census reports each person's parents' birthplaces and (for women) number of children born and surviving — data absent from earlier enumerations. Patrick Flynn (born ~1845) would be ~55 and heading his own household; his parents' birthplace columns would corroborate Ireland as the origin for both father and mother, and if Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, age ~82) is still living he may appear in Patrick's household with his relationship explicitly stated. The 1900 census also records years of immigration and years of marriage, which could distinguish Thomas Flynn's family from other same-name men in the county. The proof summary (ps_001) identifies this census as a primary gap. Try name variants: Flinn, Flynd.

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife is required for this parentage question. No source found to date names Patrick's mother; her identity is the primary open gap. This marriage record: (a) confirms Thomas and his wife as a couple; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name, which census and death records entirely omit; and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845) corroborates Thomas as the father who is otherwise named only by indirect census co-residence (1850, 1860) and the secondary death-certificate informant. Note the limit: the marriage record establishes the couple's union but does not by itself place Patrick as their child — that link still rests on the household evidence. collections_search returned collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (personCount 982,415, indexed, 1708–1985), covering Schuylkill County Catholic and other parish registers. The locality guide notes that Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868; this collection covers that pre-Scranton period. Thomas (born ~1818) and Patrick (born ~1845) suggest a marriage window of 1835–1850. Try variants: Flinn, Flynd, Flynn; search both surname fields.

Fallback for pli_009. If Thomas Flynn's marriage is not found in the indexed SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection, browse image group 007936751 (Church Records 1842–1895, Schuylkill County, 0% indexed, bilingual English/German — returned by volume_search). The marriage is expected in a Catholic parish register pre-dating the 1868 creation of the Diocese of Scranton; this volume spans the relevant period. Browse for a Flynn/Flinn marriage entry naming a bride whose surname would identify Patrick's mother. The bilingual nature of the volume reflects the mixed Irish-German anthracite coal community; check both English and German-language register sections.

A search for baptism records of Thomas Flynn's children in Schuylkill County Catholic parish registers. Baptism entries name both parents — they are direct parentage evidence for any child listed. Finding a sibling of Patrick who was baptized in Schuylkill County would directly confirm Thomas and his wife (with her maiden name) as parents, supporting the conclusion that Patrick is also their child. collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (personCount 982,415, indexed, 1708–1985) is the primary source. Date range 1840–1870 covers children who could have been born before Patrick (~1845, first child found in household) and those born after him. The date range is sized to Thomas Flynn's plausible child-bearing window as creator of these records, not to Patrick's own window. Variant spellings: Flynn, Flinn, Flynd.

The proof summary (ps_001) explicitly identifies Thomas Flynn's probate records as a primary remaining gap. A will naming Patrick as a son would be the strongest direct parentage evidence currently missing from the record set; an intestate administration would name the heirs, which could include Patrick and could name Thomas's surviving wife (Patrick's mother). collections_search returned collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994; personCount 0 — not indexed) and volume_search returned image group 007936749 (Probate Records 1851–1930, Schuylkill County, 0% indexed). This must be executed as an image browse of the county Register of Wills dockets, not a name search. Thomas was born ~1818; the date range 1865–1912 reflects his plausible death window (age 47–94), sized to the creator's lifespan rather than to Patrick's research window. Note: if Thomas survived past 1906, a Pennsylvania state death certificate would also exist naming his spouse; search FamilySearch Pennsylvania death certificates 1906–1915 alongside the probate browse.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage record may name his parents. The 1908 death certificate informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law — confirming Patrick had at least one daughter who married, and implying Patrick himself married. Some Pennsylvania marriage records from this era name the parents of both parties. Search first in the indexed collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (982,415 persons, Catholic and other parish registers, 1708–1985) for a Catholic church marriage; then browse image group 007936753 (Marriage Records 1870–1910, Schuylkill County, 0% indexed) for civil marriage registration (Pennsylvania required county-level recording from 1885). If Patrick's marriage record names Thomas Flynn as his father, it provides an independent statement of parentage in addition to the death certificate's secondary informant. Date range 1865–1900 reflects Patrick's plausible marriage window (age 20–55); sized to Patrick as the record's subject.

Thomas Flynn was born in Ireland and was in Schuylkill County by 1850 (age 32, Ireland, head of household). His naturalization declaration or petition may name his wife and children — common in some pre-1906 naturalization documents — and may identify his county or parish of origin in Ireland, which could open a parallel Irish research path. volume_search returned image group 007936750 (Naturalization Records 1849–1915, Schuylkill County, 0% indexed). This must be executed as an image browse of the county court naturalization dockets. Date range 1849–1880 covers from the earliest volume date through a plausible end of Thomas's active period; sized to Thomas's lifespan as the record creator, not Patrick's research window. The locality guide flags that some naturalization films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only — confirmed by the 0% indexed result.

Deed records for Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County may name Patrick or other children as grantees in property transfers, supply Thomas's wife's name in a co-grantor signature (wives routinely joined deeds to release dower rights in Pennsylvania), or name witnesses and adjoining landowners who were FAN members. volume_search returned image group 007936752 (Deed Records 1815–1900, Schuylkill County, 22% indexed — partially name-searchable). Run a name search (Flynn, Flinn) against the indexed 22% first; then browse images for the 1845–1900 window to cover the unindexed majority. Boundary recitals in deeds name adjoining landowners by definition — a FAN-research source. Date range 1845–1900 spans Thomas's period in Schuylkill County through the end of the volume's coverage.

FAN item — required for a parentage question (BCG Standard 14). Other Flynn households in Schuylkill County in the 1870 and 1880 censuses may represent Thomas Flynn's brothers, cousins, or fellow-townland emigrants from Ireland. Their households could name Thomas's wife (Patrick's mother) directly, or identify her family's surname by showing their own wives with Irish surnames — particularly valuable because no US source yet names Patrick's mother. The 1880 census is especially useful because it states relationships, allowing kin clusters among the Flynns to be mapped. What this reveals about the subject: a FAN-connected Flynn household in the same county may preserve the maternal maiden name or family identity that Patrick's own records omit. Search FamilySearch 1870 and 1880 census indexes for all Flynn / Flinn households in Schuylkill County, then compare household compositions and wives' names against what the earlier items reveal about Thomas's family.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes moved from the Diocese of Philadelphia to the Diocese of Scranton in 1868. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County

entry.rationale: Bridget Halloran married John Doyle (first husband); one child already identified (Ellen Doyle). Goal: enumerate all other children of this union. Schuylkill County, PA, ~1838–1900. No statewide civil birth/death registration before 1906 (loc_001); pre-1906 vital events depend on census, church, cemetery, and probate records. Catholic parishes were under Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868, then Diocese of Scranton. Some coal-region church films are browse-only (vol 007936751). Probate records available from county Register of Wills from 1811 (browse-only, vol 007936749). Plan searches free FamilySearch sources first, then Ancestry. Censuses with co-resident children are highest-probability sources; baptism registers listing parents and John Doyle's probate are the next tier.

The 1860 US Federal Census (collection 1473181, personCount 27,518,891 — indexed) is the highest-probability source for capturing the intact Doyle household with all co-residing children enumerated by name and age. If John Doyle was still alive in 1860, the household would list him as head, Bridget as wife, and all children then living at home. Search for 'John Doyle' in Schuylkill County, PA; also search 'Bridget Doyle' in case John had died. Note Halloran variant spellings (Halloran, Halleren, Halloran) when searching Bridget.

The 1870 US Federal Census (collection 1438024, personCount 38,558,371 — indexed). If John Doyle had died before 1870, Bridget may appear as a widow with surviving Doyle children still at home, or she may have remarried (as implied by 'first husband'). Search for Bridget under both Doyle and any remarriage surname, and for Doyle-surnamed children as heads of their own households. Cross-reference ages with 1860 findings.

The 1880 US Federal Census (collection 1417683, personCount 50,169,452 — indexed). The 1880 schedule specifies each person's relationship to the head of household, aiding identification of adult Doyle children who may now head their own families. Search for Doyle-surnamed individuals in Schuylkill County and adjacent counties (Carbon, Northumberland, Columbia) in case any children migrated to nearby coal towns.

The 1900 US Federal Census (collection 1325221, personCount 76,211,837 — indexed). By 1900 all Doyle children born by ~1882 would be adults. The 1900 schedule records exact birth month/year and, for married women, number of children born and surviving — useful corroboration. Search for known Doyle children and any new candidates identified from earlier censuses. The 1900 schedule also lists parents' birthplaces, which can confirm Irish parentage consistent with Bridget Halloran.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, personCount 982,415 — indexed, name-searchable). Covers 1708–1985. Search for baptisms/christenings listing John Doyle as father and Bridget Halloran (or variants) as mother. Per loc_001, Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868 and the Diocese of Scranton thereafter; records may be filed under either diocese. Search variant spellings: Doyle, Doyel; Halloran, Hallerin, Hallaran.

Browse-only church records: FamilySearch image group 007936751 (Church Records 1842–1895, 187 images, 0% indexed, languages: English and German). Per loc_001 quirk, some coal-region church films are browse-only and will not appear in the indexed SYNTH-PA-CHURCH search. This volume likely covers parishes not captured in the indexed collection. Browse page-by-page for Doyle baptism entries. If the indexed search (pli_005) returns complete results for the relevant parishes, this browse may be abbreviated.

John Doyle's probate or estate administration record at the Schuylkill County Register of Wills would name his heirs — typically all surviving children — making this potentially the single most comprehensive source for enumerating children. FamilySearch image group 007936749 (Probate Records 1851–1930, 412 images, 0% indexed — browse-only); also collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994, browse-only images). Date window set to John Doyle's plausible death range: as Bridget's 'first husband' he predeceased her, most likely between ~1840 and ~1895. Browse for 'Doyle' in the probate dockets. Lifespan of the record creator (John Doyle) sets the window bounds.

Browse-only marriage records: FamilySearch image group 007936753 (Marriage Records 1870–1910, 94 images, 0% indexed). Marriage records of Doyle children would name their parents (John Doyle and Bridget Halloran), providing direct evidence of each child's parentage. Date window reflects when children born 1838–1882 would plausibly marry (roughly age 18+). Browse for 'Doyle' grooms and brides and check parent fields. Any Doyle child who married in Schuylkill County before 1910 may appear here.

1850 US Federal Census — Schuylkill County (Ancestry collection 1276, per external_links_search). The 1850 census is the earliest federal enumeration available and would show the Doyle household at its earliest snapshot, including Ellen and any older siblings. FamilySearch did not return a 1850 US census collection in this session's scope query; Ancestry holds this record set. Date window: 1850. Search for 'John Doyle' in Schuylkill County. Note: the 1850 schedule does not list relationships to head, so all co-residents with the same surname are candidates.

FAN cluster — Ellen Doyle (the one known child of Bridget Halloran and John Doyle). Ellen's death certificate (if post-1906, Pennsylvania civil registration), marriage record, obituary, or probate may name surviving siblings, providing the most direct corroboration of the sibling group. Search FamilySearch for Ellen Doyle death/marriage records in Schuylkill County and surrounding area. Also search newspapers for an obituary that might list surviving brothers and sisters. This item reveals evidence about the other children through the known child's own records.

If John Doyle was still alive in 1860, the household would list him as head, Bridget as wife, and all children then living at home. Search for 'John Doyle' in Schuylkill County, PA; also search 'Bridget Doyle' in case John had died. Note Halloran variant spellings (Halloran, Halleren, Hallaran) when searching Bridget.

The 1870 US Federal Census (collection 1438024, personCount 38,558,371 — indexed). If John Doyle had died before 1870, Bridget may appear as a widow with surviving Doyle children still at home, or she may have remarried (as implied by 'first husband'). Search for Bridget under both Doyle and any remarriage surname, and for Doyle-surnamed children as heads of their own households. Cross-reference ages with 1860 findings.

The 1880 US Federal Census (collection 1417683, personCount 50,169,452 — indexed). The 1880 schedule specifies each person's relationship to the head of household, aiding identification. Search for Doyle-surnamed individuals in Schuylkill County and adjacent counties (Carbon, Northumberland, Columbia) in case any children migrated to nearby coal towns.

The 1900 US Federal Census (collection 1325221, personCount 76,211,837 — indexed). By 1900 all Doyle children born by ~1882 would be adults. The 1900 schedule records exact birth month/year and, for married women, number of children born and surviving — useful corroboration. Also lists parents' birthplaces, confirming Irish parentage consistent with Bridget Halloran.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, personCount 982,415 — indexed, name-searchable). Search for baptisms/christenings listing John Doyle as father and Bridget Halloran (or variants) as mother. Per loc_001, Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868 and the Diocese of Scranton thereafter; records may be filed under either diocese. Search variant spellings: Doyle, Doyel; Halloran, Hallerin, Hallaran.

John Doyle's probate or estate administration at the Schuylkill County Register of Wills would name all surviving heirs — the most comprehensive single enumeration of children possible. FamilySearch image group 007936749 (Probate Records 1851–1930, 412 images, 0% indexed — browse-only); also collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994, browse-only images). entry.rationale: Elena's 1712 marriage to Jöns Jönsson in Västra Karaby is the project's best-documented anchor. The national Sweden Marriages index (collection 1520596, personCount 3,603,816 — name-searchable, collections_search 2026-10-02) covers 1630–1920. A Swedish marriage record of this period often names the bride's home parish, directly bearing on the birth-origin question. Search using name variants Elena, Helena, Elin, Lena; -dotter may be abbreviated d., dr., dtr. (Sweden_Naming_Customs wiki).

The national Sweden Baptisms index (collection 1520594, personCount 20,057,677 — name-searchable, collections_search 2026-10-02) covers 1611–1920. Elena's patronymic Asmundsdotter confirms her father was Asmund; a baptism entry would name both parents and the baptizing parish. Caution: the Västra Karaby register begins 1688 (loc_002); a birth before that date has no baptism entry in this parish. Search using name variants Elena, Helena, Elin, Lena, with father given name Asmund (also Åsmund), c. 1685–1700. A nil result may indicate a pre-1688 birth or origin from a neighboring parish.

For a parentage question, the candidate parents' marriage to each other is a required plan item. Asmund Jönsson (I3) is the candidate father inferred from Elena's patronymic. His marriage entry in the national Sweden Marriages index (collection 1520596, name-searchable) would identify Elena's mother and may give a place of residence or home parish. Date window 1678–1698 is set by Asmund's plausible lifespan as father of a child born c. 1685–1695. Broadened to county (Malmöhus) because the marriage may have occurred in a parish other than Västra Karaby.

All FamilySearch volumes for Västra Karaby are 0% name-indexed (volume_search 2026-10-02; loc_002). Image group 004523018 (777 images) covers church records 1688–1804, including household examination records (husförhörslängder), baptisms, marriages and burials. Image groups 004523021_001–004 (587 images combined) cover 1662–1850 with detailed 1687–1729 sub-coverage; also includes Saxtorp parish, filmed in the same roll. Browse for: (a) Elena's baptism c. 1685–1700; (b) Asmund Jönsson's household in the husförhörslängder, which list all household members and directly address parentage; (c) Elena's 1712 marriage entry to verify home parish annotation. The Malmöhus Church Records collection (1974200) is browse-only, personCount 0 (collections_search 2026-10-02).

Household tax lists (mantalslängder) survive from 1658 for Harjager härad and are held at Riksarkivet (sok.riksarkivet.se/mantalslangder, external_links_search 2026-10-02; loc_002). These predate the 1688 parish register start and may place Asmund Jönsson in Västra Karaby with his household — including Elena — before her baptism window. This is also the FAN-cluster item required for a parentage question: neighbors recorded in the same roll corroborate the family's presence, and any co-resident with the surname Asmundsdotter or Jönsson may extend the family network. Window set by härad-level coverage from 1658 through Elena's 1712 marriage.

Swedish burial entries routinely record the deceased's age and sometimes the home parish of origin. The national Sweden Burials index (collection 1520597, personCount 2,861,902 — name-searchable, collections_search 2026-10-02) covers 1649–1920. An entry for Elena after 1712 may yield her approximate birth year and origin parish, indirectly addressing the birth-place question. This item is required by the breadth self-check: the Västra Karaby register begins only in 1688, so a baptism entry may not exist for a pre-1688 birth; Elena's own burial is the next-best evidence for her birth year and origin.

Asmund Jönsson (I3, candidate father) likely died between 1695 and 1740 — window set by his plausible lifespan as father of a child born c. 1685–1695. His burial record in the Sweden Burials index (collection 1520597, name-searchable) may state his age, home parish, and surviving family, providing corroborating evidence of his relationship to Elena. This is the mandatory FAN-cluster item for a parentage question: a candidate parent's death record bears directly on the question's subject by confirming identity and place of residence. Broadened to county because Asmund's death parish is unknown.

ArkivDigital (arkivdigital.se, external_links_search 2026-10-02) offers digitized Swedish parish registers for Malmöhus county, sometimes with better image quality or additional volumes not yet on FamilySearch. If the FamilySearch browse (pli_004) yields no baptism for Elena or no household entry for Asmund, ArkivDigital is the next repository for Västra Karaby and neighboring Saxtorp and Harjager parish registers across the 1662–1720 window.
